processing: As with other Yunnan raw pu-erh, the leaf is typically wilted, wok-fired, rolled and sun-dried into mao cha, then sold loose or steamed and pressed; no ripe-style pile fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as is usual for Mengku raw pu-erh; little is documented about the season here beyond that.
appearance_dry: Well-formed cakes of plump yellow-green strands, with bright silvery buds touched with gold.
appearance_wet: Plump buds and thick leaves in soft yellow-green, as with other Mengku large-leaf raw teas.
taste_profile: Honey sweetness and clear florals with an oily, full texture and very little bitterness or astringency; aroma lingers in the empty cup.

brewing.notes: This leaf is gentle for Mengku, so steeps can run slightly longer than for harder raw teas once it opens.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, mostly as spring tea in pressed cakes, with rattan-tea leaf named on the label. Young cakes are the usual purchase, and aged ones should state their year. Ask whether the leaf is truly from Banuo's rattan gardens, because that is the reason for the price.
description:
Banuo is the largest village on Mengku's eastern half-mountain, over 1,900 metres up, and its name means one thing to pu-erh drinkers: rattan tea. These are old tea trees with long vine-like stems, dozens or hundreds to a tree, up to three or four metres long, tangling into nets between neighbours.

Leaf from these trees has round, strong buds, pale green and densely downy when fresh, white with a hint of gold once dried. It is made in the usual raw pu-erh way, and pressed cakes show the buds clearly on the surface.

The cup is known for honey more than force: yellow, glossy, sweet in the mouth, with florals rising in the aftertaste and very little bite. That softness tempts people to overbrew it, so taste as you lengthen the steeps.

Eastern half-mountain teas from the mostly Han villages often come from rattan gardens, but Banuo's is reckoned the best kept and largest. Check for the village name and for rattan-tea leaf specifically.

For contrast, try it beside a western half-mountain tea from the same area.
history:
Banuo's rattan gardens were larger before 1949 than they are now, though they remain the largest in the Shuangjiang area. One trade source says the tea once served as a tribute tea to the local chieftains; that claim has no detail attached.

Its fame today rests on these gardens, and it is well known throughout Lincang.
